summary: Specifies how to use the US National Security Agency's Suite B cryptographic algorithms with S/MIME secure email. It obsoletes RFC 5008 and is informational. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Some government agencies required a particular set of secret-code methods. This says how to use that set to protect email. It is now historic, meaning it is not in active use.

questions: which curves does suite b use
subtitle: Which NSA Suite B algorithms an S/MIME email system must use, and how to plug them into signing and encryption.

tldr.problem: Agencies that wanted to protect email with the US National Security Agency's Suite B algorithms needed one place saying exactly which algorithms S/MIME should use and how.
tldr.mechanism: It picks two matching sets of algorithms, one for 128-bit and one for 192-bit minimum security: SHA-256 or SHA-384 with ECDSA for signatures, and ECDH, AES Key Wrap and AES in CBC mode for encryption. The details are mostly inherited from other RFCs.
tldr.outcome: The document is Informational and now has Historic status. It obsoletes RFC 5008 and gave more freedom in how the two security levels are combined.

today: RFC 6318 is Historic: it is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 5008, and the metadata lists no RFC that replaces it. Read it as a record of how Suite B was applied to S/MIME, not as current guidance.

sections.title: Why Suite B for S/MIME
sections.content:
Suite B is a set of cryptographic algorithms announced by the US National Security Agency in 2005. It covers key exchange, digital signatures, hashing and the AES encryption algorithm, and all of it was selected from cryptography approved by NIST.

This RFC says how to use those algorithms in S/MIME, the secure email format, which relies on the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). Only the CMS signed-data and enveloped-data content types are involved. Other uses of CMS are out of scope.

Most of the conventions already exist in other RFCs, so this document mainly points to them and repeats relevant details. It obsoletes RFC 5008, mainly to allow more flexibility in using the Suite B security levels.
sections.plainLanguage: There was a short approved list of code-making recipes. This paper says how to use that list for email, and mostly points to other papers for the fine print.

sections.title: Two Security Levels, Two Algorithm Sets
sections.content:
Suite B defines two minimum levels of cryptographic security, 128 and 192 bits. For signing it offers two Sig Sets: Sig Set 1 pairs SHA-256 with ECDSA on curve P-256, and Sig Set 2 pairs SHA-384 with ECDSA on P-384.

For encryption it offers two KE Sets. KE Set 1 uses ECDH with P-256, a SHA-256 key derivation function, AES-128 Key Wrap and AES-128 CBC. KE Set 2 uses P-384, SHA-384, AES-256 Key Wrap and AES-256 CBC.

At a 128-bit minimum, a system that encrypts MUST use KE Set 1 or KE Set 2, with KE Set 1 preferred. Any signature MUST use Sig Set 1 or Sig Set 2, independent of the encryption choice. At a 192-bit minimum, encryption MUST use KE Set 2 and signatures MUST use Sig Set 2.

Recipients must be able to check signatures too. At the 128-bit level a recipient MUST verify Sig Set 1 and SHOULD verify Sig Set 2. At the 192-bit level it MUST verify Sig Set 2.
sections.plainLanguage: There are a small and a big version of the same toolkit. You choose how strong you need to be, and then you use the toolkit that matches.

sections.title: Hashing and Signing
sections.content:
SHA-256 and SHA-384 are the Suite B message digest (hash) algorithms, used following the conventions in RFC 5754. When creating them, implementations MUST leave the AlgorithmIdentifier parameters absent, though they MUST accept both absent and NULL parameters.

ECDSA, the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, is the signature algorithm, following RFC 5753. The identifiers are ecdsa-with-SHA256 and ecdsa-with-SHA384, and their parameters field MUST be absent. The two signature values r and s MUST be sent together as an ECDSA-Sig-Value sequence of two integers.

Certificates used to verify S/MIME signatures MUST comply with the Suite B Certificate Profile in RFC 5759.
sections.plainLanguage: Hashing squeezes a message into a short fingerprint, and signing locks that fingerprint with your private stamp so others can check it came from you.

sections.title: Key Agreement, Key Wrap and Key Derivation
sections.content:
Suite B for S/MIME MUST use ephemeral-static ECDH key agreement. The sender makes a fresh ephemeral key pair, and the recipient has a static key pair whose public key is in an X.509 certificate that follows RFC 5759. This fits S/MIME's store-and-forward nature.

The shared secret Z goes through a key derivation function based on SHA-256 (KE Set 1) or SHA-384 (KE Set 2). Z MUST be exactly 256 bits for KE Set 1 and 384 bits for KE Set 2. One iteration is enough, with the counter fixed at 0x00000001. The key-encryption key is the most significant 128 bits of the SHA-256 output, or the most significant 256 bits of the SHA-384 output.

That key-encryption key then wraps the content-encryption key with AES Key Wrap (id-aes128-wrap or id-aes256-wrap). The derivation input includes a length field that MUST be 0x00000080 for a 128-bit key and 0x00000100 for a 256-bit key.

The only secret input to the derivation is Z. If the optional user keying material is different for every message, a different key-encryption key is produced for each message.
sections.plainLanguage: Sender and receiver each combine a secret of their own with the other one's public part to get the same secret, then use it to lock the box that holds the real message key.

sections.title: Content Encryption with AES CBC
sections.content:
The message body itself is encrypted with AES in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode, following RFC 3565. With KE Set 1 it MUST be AES-128 CBC (id-aes128-CBC), and with KE Set 2 it MUST be AES-256 CBC (id-aes256-CBC).

The algorithm parameters field MUST be present and contain a 16-octet initialization vector, which the sender generates at random.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is scrambled with a lock whose strength matches the key set you picked, and each message starts from a fresh random twist so locks never repeat.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Every algorithm and identifier here was defined in earlier documents, so this RFC adds no new cryptography. It says only that the two minimum security levels exist and that users must weigh their own risk environment to choose between them. It also points to RFC 4086 for guidance on generating random values.

For deeper analysis it refers to the security considerations of RFC 5652 (CMS), RFC 3370 (CMS algorithms), RFC 5753 (ECC in CMS) and RFC 3565 (AES in CMS).
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is invented here. You pick how strong a lock you need, and the older papers explain how each part stays safe.
